title: Rise Early on October 22nd for the Orionid Meteor Shower
excerpt: The Moon bugs out just in time to enjoy the peak of the Orionids, which trace their origin to Halley's Comet.
content:
The Moon bugs out just in time to enjoy the peak of the Orionids, which trace their origin to Halley’s Comet.

Orion is a favorite constellation for many. Its conspicuous Belt and numerous bright stars make an indelible impression. As a child, I remember standing on my bed in pajamas looking out the window — shade tucked behind my head — watching the celestial Hunter climb over the next-door neighbor's roof on January nights. I pointed my 2.4-inch refractor this way to see my very first nebula. Later, I learned that a meteor shower — the Orionids — sprang from the constellation every October, and that the zippy flashes were pieces of Halley's Comet. How could a single constellation be this wonderful?

Perhaps you'll recall a happy Orion memory while you're bundled up on a lounge chair, staring up at the sky waiting for the Hunter to share his meteoric quarry. The annual shower peaks the night of October 21–22, when you might spot about 20 meteors per hour from a dark, moonless sky. Although Orion's up in the southeast by midnight, the 82% waxing gibbous Moon in Aquarius washes out the sky until setting around 3 a.m. Thereafter, until the start of dawn — a span of nearly 3 hours — dark skies ideal for meteor-watching return. Although Orionids dash anywhere they please, all of them originate from a radiant in Orion's upraised club.

The radiant is a vanishing point where parallel lines appear to come to a point. Artists use it in paintings to create the illusion of three dimensions on a flat surface. Similarly, in the sky, Orionid meteors appear to come from a point but actually travel on parallel paths when they enter Earth's atmosphere. The mostly sand-sized particles strike at high velocity (66 kilometers per second), just slightly slower than the Leonids (71 km/s), the fastest of the annual showers. Rapid air compression along the particle's path heats the surrounding air to around 3,000° C (5,400° F), hot enough to knock electrons off both the meteoroid and atoms and create an ionized "tube" of radiant plasma — a meteor streak.

One reason Orionids come in hot is that their parent, Halley's Comet, revolves around the Sun in retrograde, opposite of the planets. Debris boiled off from solar heating each time the comet approaches the Sun likewise travels in retrograde. When Earth crosses the comet's orbit in October, the particles and our planet collide nearly head-on at high velocity, and Orionids rip across the sky!

The shower is an ancient one. In their 1989 paper The Age of the Orionid Meteor Stream, J. Jones et al. hypothesized that the present Orionids originated during the comet's close approach to Jupiter around 23,000 years ago. Ongoing interactions with the giant planet through resonances cause the debris to clump together into denser strands. When Earth crosses a filament, we see a stronger shower. The earliest confirmed observations of the shower come from Chinese and Japanese records around 585 A.D. That year, activity was particularly strong with “hundreds of meteors scattered in all directions" reported. 

Oddly, Western astronomers weren't aware of the shower until the 1830s. American amateur scientist Edward C. Herrick called attention to a possible new shower after observing a strong increase in meteor numbers in mid-October 1839 and again in 1840. Astronomers Adolphe Quetelet and Johann Benzenberg recorded similar activity around the same time and are regarded as independent co-discoverers. Alexander Herschel, grandson of William Herschel, determined the radiant from observations in 1864 and 1865. For a fun and fascinating read about Herrick's role in co-discovering the Perseids and their radiant, I highly recommend this 2005 Sky & Telescope article.

Keep an eye on betelgeuse, too!

The Orionids are active from October 2nd through November 7th, so if it's cloudy, watch the morning before or after. As you scan the sky for the next meteor, keep an eye on Betelgeuse. In the Astronomer's Telegram #18097 posted Oct. 8th, Daniel Jadlovsky (Masaryk University) and his colleagues postulate the star may be headed for another Great Dimming like that in 2019–2020, when the red supergiant dipped to magnitude 1.6, a historical low. It's currently at magnitude 1.0 and fading. You can use Aldebaran, or Alpha Tauri (magnitude 0.9) and neighboring Bellatrix, or Gamma Orionis (1.6) as comparison stars to keep track of the fidgety star.

I leave you with this bit of practical advice from Herrick on the proper way to observe meteor showers — "Shooting stars must always be watched in the open air: observations through a window can not be trusted." I couldn't agree more!

About Bob King

I love the sky (day and night) and have been a skywatcher and amateur astronomer since childhood. I'm also a long-time member of the American Association of Variable Star Observers (AAVSO) and Astronomical League. I pen the Astro Bob blog and have written four books: Night Sky with the Naked Eye (2016); Wonders of the Night Sky You Must See Before You Die (2018) and Urban Legends from Space (2019) and Magnificent Aurora, published in 2024. The universe invites us on an adventure every single night. To accept the invitation, we only need look up.
